title: The wick drawn down
hookLine: Patacara watches the lamp's wick pulled down and the flame go out, and is free (Therigatha, Patacara)

cards: Night. A small hut. A clay lamp burning beside a bed.
A woman sits down on the bed and takes up a needle. She reaches into the lamp, draws the wick down, and the flame goes out. In the Therigatha, that is the moment Patacara's mind comes free.
The path met her before, as the woman who lost everything and became a teacher of grieving women. The commentary says she taught Uttama too. Today, her own poem, and the lamp at the center of it.

teach.b: First, her question. The poem opens in the fields: men plow and sow seed, and gain wealth to support their wives and children.
Then Patacara asks: I keep the precepts, I do what the Teacher taught, I'm not lazy and I'm not proud. Why haven't I come free? It's an honest complaint, and the poem keeps it.
She washes her feet and watches the water run down the slope. She steadies her mind, the way a good horse is trained. Third, the lamp.

teach.h: A NEEDLE DRAWS THE WICK DOWN.
teach.b: She takes a lamp into her dwelling, looks over the bed, sits down, takes a needle, and draws down the wick. Fourth, the word. Like the going out of the lamp, the poem says, was the release of her mind.
And the Pali word for the lamp going out is nibbana, the same word the tradition uses for the goal of the whole path. In this poem it isn't abstract at all.
It's a flame in a clay lamp, and a woman with a needle, watching it go. No one blows it out. The wick is drawn down, and the flame has nothing left to hold onto.
The poem doesn't explain the image. It sets the small act of putting a lamp out for the night beside the freedom the whole path aims at, and lets them sit together.

how: Buddhist teachers use the image of a lamp going out when explaining nibbana, and in Theravada communities Patacara's verse is read as a picture of it, told by a woman who had known great loss.

o: a flame going out; the path's goal
a deep trance that lasts for days
a heaven where the awakened live on

s: Patacara's poem pictures freedom as a lamp going out
like the going out of the lamp, the poem says, was the release of her mind.
the poem says she had been lazy before she came free
she says she isn't lazy or proud, and asks why she still hasn't come free.
she comes free while teaching a large crowd
she's alone in her dwelling at night, with a needle and a lamp.

games.q: Patacara has washed her feet and watched the water run down the slope. now she takes a lamp into her dwelling and sits on the bed. what does she do with the lamp?
o: reads by it late into the night.
takes a needle and draws down the wick.
carries it out to the other nuns.
games.why: she sits, takes a needle and draws down the wick. as the flame goes out, her mind comes free.

practice: If a candle is nearby and it's safe, light it, watch it for a few breaths, then put it out and watch the last of the smoke rise.
If not, dim a lamp, or close your eyes and wait for one thought to end on its own, the way a flame ends when nothing feeds it. Then rest in the quiet after it.

wordCard.voice: Nibbana. The going out of a lamp's flame, the very word Patacara's poem uses as her mind comes free. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali nibbāna (Sanskrit nirvāṇa): the going out of a flame; the word the tradition uses for the goal of the path.

carryVoice: Your line: the flame goes out. A lamp put out for the night, and a mind set free. Day seven hundred eighty-six, done.

sources.ref: Therigatha commentary on Uttama (Patacara as her teacher)
